abstract.p: This work describes a hybrid micro-electro-mechanical-systems (MEMS) microphone integrating capacitive and piezoelectric transduction mechanisms for signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement. A theoretical system-level model was established to characterize the hybrid device, which was fabricated using a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer-based process. The piezoelectric transduction component employs a Si/SiO2/Au/AlN/Pt material stack, while the capacitive transduction part consists of a variable capacitor formed by a silicon handle layer and a silicon device layer. Experimental results at 1 kHz show that the hybrid MEMS microphone achieves sensitivities of −64.3 dB (re: 1 V/Pa) in piezoelectric mode, −54.9 dB (re: 1 V/Pa) in capacitive mode, and −52.4 dB (re: 1 V/Pa) in hybrid mode, with corresponding SNR values of 65.7 dB, 59.8 dB, and 62.2 dB, respectively. To enhance the overall SNR of the hybrid MEMS microphone, a signal fusion technique is applied to the dual synchronized signals, resulting in an enhanced SNR of 66.7 dB, exhibiting a 14.1 dB improvement compared to the 52.6 dB reported in previous work.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Recently, microelectromechanical system (MEMS) sensors have been widely used in many different fields1–3, Among them, MEMS microphones are acoustic sensing devices that have been employed in various applications, including earphones, mobile phones, laptops, and other consumer electronics4,5, MEMS microphones exhibit several key advantages compared to electret condenser microphones (ECM), such as miniaturized sizes6, excellent electro-acoustical performance7, outstanding environmental compatibility8, and low-cost batch fabrication feasibility9. Piezoelectric and capacitive transduction techniques are the two main methods used in MEMS microphones10.

Piezoelectric MEMS microphone features a single membrane structure, which consists of a structural material/metal/piezoelectric/metal layers stack11,12, The performance of the piezoelectric MEMS microphone highly depends on the piezoelectric thin film. Lead zirconate titanate (PZT)13,14, zinc oxide (ZnO)15, and aluminum nitride (AlN)16,17, are the most commonly used piezoelectric materials. By doping AlN film with Scandium, the performance of MEMS microphone can be further improved18, at the expense of a challenging fabrication process. Novel structural designs and optimization can also be employed to improve the microphone performance19,20.

Capacitive MEMS microphone typically consists of a deformable diaphragm and a backplate forming a variable capacitor, which serve as the movable and fixed electrodes, respectively21,22, The air gap and the acoustic perforations play an important role in the performance of MEMS capacitive microphones22. Using new materials for diaphragm fabrication is an efficient method to improve the device performance21,23,24. Optimization of the device structure can also be a useful approach25,26.

MEMS microphones using individual transduction technology, either piezoelectric or capacitive transduction mechanisms, depend on novel structural designs and the use of new materials to improve device performance. Integrating multiple transduction principles in a single device is a promising approach for performance enhancement. In our previous work, a PZT-based hybrid MEMS microphone combining piezoelectric and capacitive transduction mechanisms has been reported to improve the sensitivity27. However, the overall signal-to-noise ratio in hybrid mode is limited by the high noise floor of piezoelectric transduction.

This work presents a hybrid MEMS microphone using aluminum nitride (AlN) film as piezoelectric material, which is beneficial to further improve the microphone performance28. Signal fusion techniques for multi-modal sensors are employed to enhance the overall SNR of the hybrid device29. In Section II, the lumped element model of the hybrid device is established and compared with the finite element simulation results. Section III presents the fabrication technique for the AlN-based hybrid microphone. Experimental characterizations of the hybrid microphone are presented in Section IV. Conclusions are given in Section V.

sec.title: Device Structure and Lumped Element
sec.p:
A hybrid microphone 3D structure view is demonstrated in Fig. 1a. The piezoelectric diaphragm consists of a silicon layer, a thermal oxide layer, a bottom Au electrode, an AlN film, and a top Pt electrode. The capacitive transduction structure consists of a silicon handle layer and device layer, which serve as the stationary and movable electrodes, respectively. Ring top electrodes are designed to counterbalance the moments induced by residual stress during the thin film deposition. Without proper compensation, these residual stresses could cause the membrane to deflect upward or downward due to the unbalanced moments, and in the worst case, the initial static deflection may cause membrane collapse. The diaphragm deformation under an incident sound pressure wave induces stress in the piezoelectric film and capacitance change in the capacitor. To predict the MEMS microphone behavior efficiently, the lumped element modeling technique is employed. In this analysis, the device is assumed to operate in the linear regime where the membrane displacement is significantly smaller than the nominal electrode gap. Under this small-signal approximation, nonlinear capacitive effects, gap-reduction-induced nonlinearities, and variations in bias-dependent stiffness are considered higher-order terms and are neglected. This linearization allows for a physically transparent framework that captures the dominant transduction mechanisms while maintaining analytical tractability.Fig. 1Modeling of the hybrid MEMS microphone.
a 3D structure of the hybrid microphone. b Cross-section view of hybrid microphone with electroacoustic elements. c Equivalent circuit model of the hybrid microphone

To accurately capture the multiphysics mechanics of the multilayer diaphragm, we employed the composite laminate plate theory rather than treating the stack as a homogeneous material. This approach accounts for the shifted neutral axis and the distinct elastic properties of each layer.
These equivalent parameters were then incorporated into the theoretical model for further analysis.

sec.title: Equivalent Circuit Model
COMSOL vs LEM
sec.p: To verify the proposed LEM model, the frequency response of the hybrid microphone is simulated using the finite element method (FEM) and compared to the predictions from the LEM technique.

To substantiate theoretical analysis and provide a more comprehensive physical picture of the device, we have performed FEM multiphysics simulations, as shown in Fig. 3, including displacement profile (Fig. 3a), modal shape (Fig. 3b), stress distribution (Fig. 3c), and air-gap pressure fields (Fig. 3d). Obtaining the frequency response of a microphone device using the finite element method takes several hours, whereas the lumped element model provides comparable results in just a few seconds.Fig. 3FEM multiphysics outputs.
a Membrane displacement profiles. b modal shapes. c stress distribution. d air-gap pressure fields

sec.title: Fabrication
sec.p:
This section presents the fabrication process of the proposed hybrid microphone. The fabrication starts with a SOI wafer whose device and handle layers are both highly doped. The wafer is first thermal oxidized to grow a thermal oxide layer, as shown in Fig. 4a. A 250 nm Cr/Au film is deposited as the bottom electrode by sputtering, as shown in Fig. 4b. In Fig. 4c, a 600 nm thick AlN film is deposited by sputtering and patterned by lift-off process. A 300 nm Cr/Pt layer is sputtered as the top electrode and patterned by a lift-off process, as shown in Fig. 4d. In Fig. 4e, f, the Cr/Au film is etched by etching, while the thermally grown silicon oxide layer is etched by reactive ion etching (RIE). In Fig. 4g, the silicon device layer is etched by deep reactive ion etching (DRIE), and the BOX layer is etched by RIE. In the following step, Fig. 4h, the backside of the wafer was etched by DRIE to form the release holes. The final step, shown in Fig. 4i, is the etching of the sacrificial silicon oxide, which is removed in 48% hydrofluoric acid.Fig. 4Fabrication process of the proposed hybrid microphone.
a Thermal oxidation. b Cr/Au film deposition. c AlN film pattern. d Cr/Pt film pattern. e Cr/Au film etching. f Thermal oxide etching. g Silicon device layer and BOX layer etching. h Silicon handle layer DRIE etching. i Sacrificial layer etching

sec.title: Measurement Setup
Frequency Response
sec.p:
Figure 7a shows the output response signal of the hybrid device at 1 kHz for various acoustic sound pressure levels in piezoelectric, capacitive, and hybrid transduction modes. The response slope in the hybrid transduction mode is 2.39 mV/Pa, higher than 0.61 mV/Pa in the purely piezoelectric transduction mode and 1.79 mV/Pa in the capacitive transduction mode. Figure 7b presents the measured frequency response of the proposed hybrid microphone compared to the theoretical values under a 1 Pa sound pressure level in piezoelectric, capacitive, and hybrid transduction modes, using 1 V/Pa as the reference value. The frequency response of the device was measured from 100 Hz to 10 kHz. By combining both output signals, the sensitivity is enhanced across the whole frequency band of interest compared to the individual piezoelectric and capacitive transduction modes. The indicated sensitivities of the hybrid device at 1 kHz for 94 dB SPL in the piezoelectric, capacitive, and hybrid transduction modes are −64.3 dB, −54.9 dB, and −52.4 dB (re: 1 V/Pa), respectively. The experimental and theoretical results match well with each other over the band of interest. The discrepancies between theoretical and measured results can be attributed to several factors, such as fabrication tolerances and residual film stress. The residual film stress was characterized at the wafer level, local stress variations across the wafer may lead to non-uniform stress distributions in individual dies, resulting in device-to-device performance differences. The downward trend of the measured curves at high frequencies could be caused by the increased squeeze-film damping.Fig. 7Experimental characterization of the hybrid microphone.
a Measured output signal at 1 kHz for various acoustic sound pressure levels. b Frequency response compared to theoretical values. c Measured noise density. Linearity in d linear scale and e decibel scale. f THD at 1 kHz

sec.title: Noise Floor
Linearity
sec.p: Linearity and total harmonic distortion (THD) of the microphone are measured to evaluate how the microphone output varies with sound pressure levels. The THD ratio is measured at 1 kHz sound pressure and computed based on the first six harmonic components using the included software. Figure 7d, e shows the output voltage of the DUT operating in different transduction modes under the varying reference microphone sound pressure level at 1 kHz, shown in both linear and decibel scales. The upper limit of the sound pressure level of the testing instrument is approximately 381 Pa, which corresponds to 145.6 dB SPL. Figure 7f shows the measured THD. At maximum achievable sound pressure level, microphones exhibit a THD of 2.3%, 11.23%, and 8.81% in piezoelectric, capacitive, and hybrid transduction modes, respectively. The sudden rise in THD for the capacitive mode might be because the diaphragm displacement at high SPLs reaches several hundred nanometers, driving the capacitive response into a nonlinear regime.

sec.title: Signal Fusion
sec.p: The capacitive and piezoelectric paths respond to the same acoustic excitation, making their signal components coherent, while their noise sources are statistically uncorrelated, verified by calculating the correlation coefficient of the noise time sequence, which is found to be close to zero. The weighted fusion algorithm acts as an optimal estimator: it reduces the contribution of the noisier path, minimizing the total noise power while retaining the useful signal from both channels. Because coherent signal components add linearly, whereas uncorrelated noise components add in power, the fusion makes the signal exceed the increase in noise. As a result, the fused output could achieve an SNR higher than that of either individual sensing mode.

The signal values of two channels are acquired from the experiment, and the optimal gain is determined by a parametric sweep during post-processing. Figure 8a demonstrates the relationship between the minimum detectable pressure (MDP) and normalized gain g, where the optimal parameter is found at g = 11.1. The optimal gain factor was derived from experimentally measured noise characteristics, which typically remain stable. Due to the flat maximum of the SNR improvement curve, the method remains robust to slight deviations in gain without significant performance loss. In practical ASICs, the optimal gain can be implemented as either a fixed calibrated value or dynamically adjusted to adapt to environmental changes.Fig. 8Signal fusion.
a Relationship between the minimum detectable pressure and gain during the signal fusion at 1 kHz. b PSD of the fused signal

Figure 8b shows the PSD of the fused signal, indicating a MDP of 27.3 dB as mentioned. The fused result demonstrates a MDP of 27.3 dB at 1 kHz, which is 6.9 dB, 1 dB, and 4.5 dB lower than that in the capacitive, piezoelectric, and hybrid modes, respectively. The calculated SNR after signal fusion is 66.7 dB, which is 1 dB and 5.9 dB higher than that in the pure piezoelectric (65.7 dB) and capacitive (59.8 dB) modes, respectively. The overall SNR after signal fusion (66.7 dB) demonstrates an improvement of 4.5 dB over that before the signal fusion (62.2 dB). Moreover, it shows a 14.1 dB enhancement compared to the value of 52.6 dB reported in the previous work27. Thus, the overall SNR of the hybrid device is improved by this simple linear signal fusion technique. Table 3 shows the performance of this work compared with other notable works.Table 3

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, this work presented an AlN-based MEMS microphone integrating piezoelectric and capacitive transduction mechanisms to improve the microphone performance. A lumped element model is established and compared to the finite element simulation results. This model characterizes the device in the linear regime, capturing the dominant behavior while neglecting higher-order nonlinear effects for analytical clarity. The silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer-based fabrication technology is introduced. The measured sensitivities of the hybrid MEMS microphone in piezoelectric, capacitive, and hybrid modes at 1 kHz are -64.3 dB, -54.9 dB, and -52.4 dB (re: 1 V/Pa), respectively. The SNR of the device in three modes at 1 kHz is 65.7 dB, 59.8 dB, and 62.2 dB, respectively. By employing the signal fusion technique, the overall SNR of the hybrid device is improved to 66.7 dB. The proposed hybrid transduction architecture suggests a promising direction for future multi-mode MEMS sensor designs. By integrating multiple transduction mechanisms within a single device and leveraging signal fusion algorithms, such designs can achieve superior performance compared to single-mode devices.
